meta.title: Who really said "If you wish to be loved, love"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Seneca did write it, in Letter 9 of his Moral Letters — but he was quoting the earlier Stoic Hecato: 'si vis amari, ama.'
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you wish to be loved, love'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely from Seneca's Letter 9 — yet Seneca himself credits the saying to Hecato of Rhodes. The real source, translation and rights.

answer.label: Written by Seneca — quoting Hecato
answer.authorDates: c. 4 BC – AD 65 · Roman Stoic philosopher, dramatist & statesman
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine line from Seneca’s ‘Moral Letters to Lucilius,’ Letter 9 — but Seneca is quoting the earlier Stoic Hecato of Rhodes: ‘si vis amari, ama.’ Richard M. Gummere’s public-domain Loeb translation renders it ‘if you would be loved, love’; the viral form ‘if you wish to be loved, love’ is a faithful, near-literal translation of the same Latin. See it at Wikisource ↗.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter 9
Hecato of Rhodes — quoted by Seneca
Richard M. Gummere, Loeb Classical Library, 1917 (‘if you would be loved, love’)

source.excerpt: Hecato says: ‘I will show you a love-charm compounded without drug, without herb, without any witch’s incantation — if you would be loved, love.’
trail: The Latin original in Seneca’s Letter 9 reads ‘Hecaton ait … si vis amari, ama’ — attributed in the text to Hecato, via latin.it ↗.
Richard M. Gummere’s public-domain Loeb translation renders the line ‘if you would be loved, love,’ expressly credited to Hecato — Wikisource ↗.
Popular quote sites drop the nuance and credit the line simply to ‘Seneca’ — e.g. Goodreads ↗.
source.excerptNote: Seneca introduces the maxim in Letter 9 to argue that a true friend is sought for the friendship itself, not for advantage — and hands the credit to Hecato, not himself.
source.rightsNote: The Latin original is ancient and long in the public domain. The standard English rendering by Richard M. Gummere (Loeb Classical Library, 1917) predates 1931 and is likewise in the U.S. public domain — it is hosted in full at Wikisource. The popular five-word form is a near-literal translation of the same Latin and carries no separate copyright.

author.name: Seneca the Younger
author.heading: About Seneca the Younger
author.metaLine: c. 4 BC – AD 65 · Roman Stoic philosopher, dramatist & statesman
author.bio: Lucius Annaeus Seneca was a Roman Stoic philosopher, tragedian and statesman who served as tutor and adviser to the emperor Nero. His Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) — 124 letters on how to live well — is his most enduring work, and the reason so many Stoic one-liners survive. In Letter 9, on friendship, he preserves this maxim by explicitly crediting it to the earlier Stoic Hecato of Rhodes, not to himself.

misattribution.heading: What actually gets misattributed
misattribution.intro: The quote is real and really is in Seneca — the confusion is about whose words they are and which English form is canonical.

items.why: In Letter 9 Seneca writes ‘Hecaton ait … si vis amari, ama’ — he explicitly names the earlier Stoic Hecato as the author and is passing the maxim along, not claiming it. Crediting only ‘Seneca’ drops the person Seneca was quoting. See Wikisource ↗.

The viral five-word form “if you wish to be loved, love” is a faithful literal translation of ‘si vis amari, ama,’ but it is not word-for-word any single canonical English edition; Gummere’s Loeb reads ‘if you would be loved, love.’

misattribution.truthLine: The maxim is genuine and genuinely sits in Seneca’s Letter 9 — but the words are Hecato’s, which Seneca himself makes clear — see the Latin text ↗.

context.heading: Why it was written
lead: Letter 9 of the Moral Letters answers a challenge from Lucilius about whether the wise man needs friends. Seneca argues that the Stoic seeks friendship not for insurance against misfortune but for its own sake — to have someone to whom he can give love and loyalty.

To clinch the point he reaches for a line from Hecato of Rhodes: the only reliable ‘love-charm’ is to love first. It is offered as borrowed wisdom, which is exactly why the modern habit of stamping it ‘— Seneca’ is only half right.
detailsBody: Hecato of Rhodes was a Stoic philosopher of the late 2nd / early 1st century BC and a pupil of Panaetius. His writings survive only in fragments and quotations — chiefly through Cicero and Seneca — which is why the maxim reaches us under Seneca’s name rather than his own.
context.pull: ‘Si vis amari, ama’ — the one love-charm that needs no herb or spell.
